“Why, surely you don't mean—” my sister began.

“Yes, I do, ma'am,” Pumblechook said. “But wait a moment. Go on, Joseph. Well done! Keep going!”

“What would everyone here think,” Joe continued, “of twenty pounds?”

“I'd call that generous,” my sister replied.

“Well, then,” said Joe, “it's more than twenty.”

That miserable hypocrite Pumblechook nodded again and gave a patronizing laugh. “More than that, ma'am. Well done again! Keep her guessing, Joseph!”

“Then to finish the matter,” said Joe, joyfully passing my sister the bag, “it's twenty-five pounds.”

“Twenty-five pounds, ma'am,” repeated that lowest of cheats, Pumblechook, rising to shake her hand. “And no more than you deserve—as I said when they asked my opinion. I wish you happiness with it!”

Had the villain stopped there, his conduct would have been bad enough. But he made his guilt far worse by taking charge of me, claiming an authority as my benefactor that outdid all his earlier crimes.

“Now, Joseph and wife,” Pumblechook said, gripping my arm above the elbow, “you see I'm someone who always finishes what he starts. This boy must be formally apprenticed at once. That's _my_ way. At once.”

“Heaven knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” my sister said, clutching the money, “we owe you a great deal.”

“Don't think of me, ma'am,” replied that devilish grain dealer. “A pleasure's a pleasure wherever you find it. But this boy—we must get his apprenticeship settled. To tell you the truth, I said I'd see to it.”

The magistrates were holding court in the nearby Town Hall, so we went straight over to have me formally apprenticed to Joe in their presence. I say we went, but Pumblechook actually pushed me along as though I'd just picked someone's pocket or set a haystack on fire. Indeed, most people in court assumed I had been caught in the act. As he shoved me ahead of him through the crowd, I heard people asking, “What's he done?” and others saying, “Young, too, but he looks a bad one, doesn't he?” Someone with a gentle, kindly face even handed me a religious pamphlet. It had a woodcut showing a wicked-looking young man draped in enough chains to resemble a whole shopful of sausages, and was titled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

I thought the Hall a strange place. Its pews were higher than church pews, with spectators leaning over them. Grand magistrates—one with powdered hair—reclined in chairs with folded arms, took snuff, fell asleep, wrote, or read newspapers. Shiny black portraits hung on the walls, looking to my untrained eye as though they were made of hard toffee and adhesive plaster.

The chain of necessity, forever producing misery, would have had to break, and the malicious fate governing it would never allow such a violation of her eternal laws. But why should I complain? Misery was the element I lived in, and only miserable things could come near me. Had Woodville been happy, I would never have known him. And how could I, sustained for so many years by tears and nourished in the dew of sorrow, hesitate to tell a story of grief and death?

Woodville had been required to travel into the country, where one delay after another prolonged his painful separation from his beautiful bride. She wrote to say she was a little ill, urging him to hurry home: the sight of his eyes would restore her health, and his companionship would be her surest medicine. He was held up for another three days before he could rush back. For reasons he could not understand, his heart anticipated disaster. No further letter had come, and he feared she had grown worse. That fear made him restless and impatient for the moment when he would see her standing before him again, radiant with beauty and health. Yet a sinister voice seemed constantly to whisper, “You will never see her as she was again.”

When he reached her home, he found it silent. He passed through several rooms, then saw a servant weeping bitterly in one of them. Almost fainting with fear, he barely managed to ask, “Is she dead?” and just caught the dreadful reply: “Not yet.” Shocking though those words were, they seemed less terrible than the answer he had expected. Knowing she still lived, that hope was still possible, brought him some relief. He remembered her letter and clung to the wild belief that his kisses, breathing warmth and love and life, could revive her spirit. She could not die with him beside her; his presence was the charm that would preserve her life.

He hurried into her sickroom. Her cheeks burned with fever, but her eyes were shut and she seemed unconscious. He folded her in his arms, pressed breathless kisses to her burning lips, and called her the tenderest names in a voice of restrained anguish. “Come back, Elinor. I'm here with you—your life, your love. Come back, my dearest. You promised me this gift: that I would bring you health. Let your sweet spirit return. You cannot die beside me. What is death? Never seeing you again? Losing someone who is part of myself, without whom I have neither memories nor a future?”

When I woke, the stars were still brilliant, and Taurus, high in the southern sky, told me the hour was midnight. Troubled dreams had filled my sleep. I fancied myself summoned to Timon's final banquet; I arrived ravenous, the dishes were uncovered, and hot water released its fruitless steam while I fled the wrath of my host, who took on Raymond's likeness. To my fevered imagination, the vessels he flung after me brimmed with foul vapour, and my friend's figure, warped by countless distortions, swelled into an enormous spectre with the mark of pestilence upon its forehead. Upward and upward the spreading shadow climbed, filling and seeming to strain beyond the adamant vault that arched over the world, enclosing and supporting it. The nightmare grew torturous. With a violent effort I cast off sleep and restored reason to its accustomed office. My earliest thought was of Perdita. I must go back to her, must sustain her, finding in despair whatever nourishment could best uphold her stricken heart, and drawing her away from grief's wild extremes through duty's stern commands and the gentle tenderness of sorrow.

The stars alone directed my steps. Turning away from the dreadful wreck of the Golden City, I struggled hard before at last escaping its bounds. Beyond the walls I encountered a party of soldiers, borrowed a horse from one, and hurried towards my sister. In that brief interval the plain had altered. The camp had been dismantled; remnants of the dispersed army gathered here and there in little groups, every countenance darkened, every movement expressing bewilderment and fear.

With a burdened heart I went into the palace and paused, afraid to step farther, to speak, or even to look. Perdita was in the middle of the hall, seated on the marble floor, her head drooping upon her breast, her hair in disorder, her fingers ceaselessly interlacing. Pale as the marble itself, her face was drawn in every feature by anguish. Seeing me, she raised her eyes in question. The faint hope in that glance was agony; speech failed before I could utter a word, and I felt a horrible smile crease my mouth. She read my expression. Her head sank once more, her fingers resumed their restless movements. At length I found my voice, but its sound frightened her. The unhappy girl had understood my look and would not for the world have had her dreadful sorrow given form and certainty by unalterable words. Indeed, she appeared anxious to turn my thoughts elsewhere. Rising from the floor, she whispered, “Hush! Clara has wept so much and is asleep now. We must not wake her.”
